sentence: Which assessment best distinguishes the two versions without treating memoir style as a universal punctuation rule?
setupText: A memoir contains the deliberate sequence: 'I called, I waited, I called again.' An editor proposes full stops after the first two clauses.
taskText: Which assessment best distinguishes the two versions without treating memoir style as a universal punctuation rule?
text: A memoir contains the deliberate sequence: 'I called, I waited, I called again.' An editor proposes full stops after the first two clauses. Which assessment best distinguishes the two versions without treating memoir style as a universal punctuation rule?
options: The commas compress the rhythm; full stops give each action its own beat.
The commas subordinate waiting to the repeated calls; full stops give all three actions independent factual status.
The commas make the final call a correction of the first; full stops remove that corrective relationship.
The commas present the sequence as an account by the narrator; full stops distance it as someone else's remembered words.
answer: The commas compress the rhythm; full stops give each action its own beat.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3461:Deliberate asyndetic clause sequence versus separate sentences
explanation: In this deliberate memoir style, the punctuation changes pacing rather than the stated actions or their source.

rationales.The commas subordinate waiting to the re: The three clauses are independent in form already; the commas do not grammatically subordinate waiting.
rationales.The commas compress the rhythm; full sto: In this deliberate memoir style, the punctuation changes pacing rather than the stated actions or their source.
rationales.The commas make the final call a correct: 'Again' marks repetition, not a correction that the punctuation would remove.
rationales.The commas present the sequence as an ac: No quotation or attribution changes; both versions remain the narrator's account.

sentence: Which distinction follows from the new sentence boundary?
setupText: Compare (1) 'It is not true that costs have fallen and services have improved.' with (2) 'It is not true that costs have fallen. Services have improved.'
taskText: Which distinction follows from the new sentence boundary?
text: Compare (1) 'It is not true that costs have fallen and services have improved.' with (2) 'It is not true that costs have fallen. Services have improved.' Which distinction follows from the new sentence boundary?
options: Both versions deny falling costs and improved services individually, rather than denying their combined occurrence.
The second version leaves both claims under the denial because the same topic continues across the full stop.
The first commits the writer to improved services, while the second leaves the truth of that improvement unresolved.
The first denies a conjunction; the second denies falling costs but asserts improved services.
answer: The first denies a conjunction; the second denies falling costs but asserts improved services.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3462:Sentence boundary changes negation scope over conjunction
explanation: The full stop ends the denial's scope before the service claim, changing the logical commitments.

rationales.Both versions deny falling costs and imp: Denying a conjunction does not separately deny each component; the revised second sentence is affirmative.
rationales.The second version leaves both claims un: Topic continuity does not keep the second independent assertion inside 'not true that'.
rationales.The first denies a conjunction; the seco: The full stop ends the denial's scope before the service claim, changing the logical commitments.
rationales.The first commits the writer to improved: The first does not separately assert improvement; the second does, rather than leaving it unresolved.

sentence: Which two-sentence revision most explicitly preserves the intended scope?
setupText: The intended claim is that Lena did resign, but not because of the criticism. The draft 'Lena didn't resign because of the criticism' risks a different reading.
taskText: Which two-sentence revision most explicitly preserves the intended scope?
text: The intended claim is that Lena did resign, but not because of the criticism. The draft 'Lena didn't resign because of the criticism' risks a different reading. Which two-sentence revision most explicitly preserves the intended scope?
options: Lena didn't resign. The criticism explains why.
Lena did resign. The criticism was not her reason.
Lena resigned because of the criticism. That was not her intention.
Lena didn't resign because of the criticism. She considered it.
answer: Lena did resign. The criticism was not her reason.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3463:Separate assertions resolve negation-versus-reason ambiguity
explanation: The first sentence affirms the event; the second negates only the proposed reason.

rationales.Lena did resign. The criticism was not h: The first sentence affirms the event; the second negates only the proposed reason.
rationales.Lena didn't resign. The criticism explai: This denies the resignation and presents criticism as the reason for that non-event.
This asserts the very causal link the writer intends to deny; intention is a different issue.
rationales.Lena didn't resign because of the critic: The original scope ambiguity remains, and considering resignation does not affirm that it occurred.

sentence: What changes when the closing quotation mark moves to the earlier boundary?
setupText: Compare: (1) 'The spokesperson said, "The doors were locked. The keys were missing."' (2) 'The spokesperson said, "The doors were locked." The keys were missing.'
taskText: What changes when the closing quotation mark moves to the earlier boundary?
text: Compare: (1) 'The spokesperson said, "The doors were locked. The keys were missing."' (2) 'The spokesperson said, "The doors were locked." The keys were missing.' What changes when the closing quotation mark moves to the earlier boundary?
options: Both claims now become unquoted narrator assertions, although the first retains the spokesperson as background context.
The keys statement becomes an unquoted narrator assertion.
The keys statement remains presented as the spokesperson's exact words because it follows the same reported event.
The narrator now paraphrases an explicitly attributed denial by the spokesperson that the keys were available.
answer: The keys statement becomes an unquoted narrator assertion.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3464:Quotation boundary changes attribution across complete sentences
explanation: Moving the closing mark ends the direct speech before the keys statement, changing its presented voice.

rationales.Both claims now become unquoted narrator: The door statement remains inside the quotation marks and is still presented as the spokesperson's words.
rationales.The keys statement remains presented as: A nearby sentence is not part of the exact quotation once the closing mark has ended it.
rationales.The narrator now paraphrases an explicit: The second version does not explicitly attribute a denial or paraphrase about the keys to the spokesperson.
rationales.The keys statement becomes an unquoted n: Moving the closing mark ends the direct speech before the keys statement, changing its presented voice.

sentence: Why are the semicolons appropriate even though their entries are not independent statements?
setupText: A research outline reads: 'We examined three questions: whether residents, including those without internet access, knew about the scheme; how applications were assessed; and why some applicants withdrew.'
taskText: Why are the semicolons appropriate even though their entries are not independent statements?
text: A research outline reads: 'We examined three questions: whether residents, including those without internet access, knew about the scheme; how applications were assessed; and why some applicants withdrew.' Why are the semicolons appropriate even though their entries are not independent statements?
options: They convert the embedded questions into independent questions while preserving the outline's declarative frame.
They separate complex list entries, not independent assertions.
They leave only the final question within the scope of 'examined', presenting the first two as established findings.
They split the first comma-marked entry into a main question and a subsidiary question about internet access.
answer: They separate complex list entries, not independent assertions.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3465:Semicolon list boundaries within embedded-question specification
explanation: The first question contains a comma-marked insertion about residents; semicolons mark the higher-level boundaries between the three questions.

rationales.They convert the embedded questions into: The entries retain embedded-question form and function as the content of the list.
rationales.They separate complex list entries, not: The first question contains a comma-marked insertion about residents; semicolons mark the higher-level boundaries between the three questions.
rationales.They leave only the final question withi: All three entries specify what was examined; the semicolons do not assert answers to the first two.
rationales.They split the first comma-marked entry: The internet-access phrase modifies 'residents' within the first question; it does not introduce another question.

sentence: Which account best explains the sequence's information structure?
setupText: A critic writes: 'A retreat? No. A recalibration: the ambition remains, but the method has changed.'
taskText: Which account best explains the sequence's information structure?
text: A critic writes: 'A retreat? No. A recalibration: the ambition remains, but the method has changed.' Which account best explains the sequence's information structure?
options: The critic suspends judgment between the two labels and offers the final clause as evidence for either reading.
The critic rejects the change of method while retaining the label 'recalibration' as a statement of future intention.
The fragments reject one label; the colon explains the replacement.
The question introduces an opponent's voice, and the remaining units are presented as a quotation of the critic's reply.
answer: The fragments reject one label; the colon explains the replacement.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3466:Rhetorical question-fragment sequence and explanatory colon
explanation: The short units stage the correction; retained ambition and changed method support the replacement label.

rationales.The critic suspends judgment between the: 'No' rejects 'retreat', so the passage does not leave the two labels equally open.
rationales.The critic rejects the change of method: The critic affirms that the method has changed and treats 'recalibration' as the current description.
rationales.The fragments reject one label; the colo: The short units stage the correction; retained ambition and changed method support the replacement label.
rationales.The question introduces an opponent's vo: The exchange can be rhetorical within one voice; the text does not attribute or quote another speaker.

sentence: Which revision preserves the shared object and the two decision-makers?
setupText: Original: 'The board approved, but the regulator later rejected, the revised timetable.' The editor wants two complete sentences with the object of each decision explicitly stated, using a pronoun where appropriate.
taskText: Which revision preserves the shared object and the two decision-makers?
text: Original: 'The board approved, but the regulator later rejected, the revised timetable.' The editor wants two complete sentences with the object of each decision explicitly stated, using a pronoun where appropriate. Which revision preserves the shared object and the two decision-makers?
options: The board approved. The regulator later rejected the revised timetable.
The board approved the revised timetable. The regulator later rejected it.
The board approved a revised timetable. The regulator later rejected a different version.
The revised timetable was approved. The board and regulator later rejected it.
answer: The board approved the revised timetable. The regulator later rejected it.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3467:Splitting coordinated clauses that share a postponed object
explanation: The final object of the original belongs to both verbs; the first sentence names it and the second refers back with 'it'.

rationales.The board approved. The regulator later: 'Approved' can be used without an expressed object, but this fails the explicit-object requirement for the board's decision.
rationales.The board approved the revised timetable: The final object of the original belongs to both verbs; the first sentence names it and the second refers back with 'it'.
This introduces a different timetable for the rejection, losing the original shared object.
rationales.The revised timetable was approved. The: This makes the board a participant in the later rejection instead of keeping approval and rejection assigned to separate decision-makers.

sentence: Which interpretation describes the unintentional change most precisely?
setupText: Original: 'The trustees expected the curator to reopen the gallery and review the display labels.' Proposed split: 'The trustees expected the curator to reopen the gallery. Review the display labels.'
taskText: Which interpretation describes the unintentional change most precisely?
text: Original: 'The trustees expected the curator to reopen the gallery and review the display labels.' Proposed split: 'The trustees expected the curator to reopen the gallery. Review the display labels.' Which interpretation describes the unintentional change most precisely?
options: The review remains grammatically governed by 'expected the curator to' because its intended performer is recoverable.
The review is now reported as an undertaking that the curator has accepted, rather than an expectation held by the trustees.
The review becomes a condition on reopening, because its separate imperative follows the statement of that expectation.
The review becomes a direct command, outside the curator's explicit expected actions.
answer: The review becomes a direct command, outside the curator's explicit expected actions.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3468:Breaking a controlled infinitive coordination changes directive status
explanation: The full stop removes the shared infinitive frame; 'Review...' now forms an imperative addressed to the reader.

rationales.The review becomes a direct command, out: The full stop removes the shared infinitive frame; 'Review...' now forms an imperative addressed to the reader.
rationales.The review remains grammatically governe: Recoverable intended meaning does not preserve the grammatical embedding after the sentence has ended.
rationales.The review is now reported as an underta: An imperative does not report acceptance of an undertaking by the curator.
rationales.The review becomes a condition on reopen: The second sentence gives no condition marker making review a prerequisite for reopening.

sentence: What does the isolated question do in relation to the first sentence?
setupText: The passage reads: 'We had secured the venue. Or had we? The contract bore no signature.'
taskText: What does the isolated question do in relation to the first sentence?
text: The passage reads: 'We had secured the venue. Or had we? The contract bore no signature.' What does the isolated question do in relation to the first sentence?
options: It asks the reader to choose a venue while preserving the narrator's certainty that a booking had been secured.
It qualifies who secured the venue while leaving the existence of a secure booking unchallenged.
It reopens the preceding assertion to doubt.
It rejects the preceding assertion as false before the unsigned contract supplies an explanation of that established falsity.
answer: It reopens the preceding assertion to doubt.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3469:Standalone elliptical question reopens a preceding assertion
explanation: The repeated auxiliary recovers the previous proposition; the unsigned contract then provides grounds for uncertainty.

rationales.It asks the reader to choose a venue whi: The question is whether the venue was secured, not which venue to choose.
rationales.It reopens the preceding assertion to do: The repeated auxiliary recovers the previous proposition; the unsigned contract then provides grounds for uncertainty.
rationales.It qualifies who secured the venue while: The subject remains 'we'; the challenge concerns successful securing, not who did it.
rationales.It rejects the preceding assertion as fa: The question suspends certainty rather than conclusively denying the booking; the final sentence supplies a reason for doubt.

sentence: How does the second unit qualify the first?
setupText: A review concludes: 'The argument is ingenious. Not that ingenuity makes it sound.'
taskText: How does the second unit qualify the first?
text: A review concludes: 'The argument is ingenious. Not that ingenuity makes it sound.' How does the second unit qualify the first?
options: It retracts the praise by treating ingenuity as a description the reviewer no longer accepts.
It offers ingenuity as a necessary condition for soundness while denying that the condition has been met.
It blocks an inference to soundness while retaining the praise.
It establishes that the argument is unsound and gives its ingenuity as the reason for that failure.
answer: It blocks an inference to soundness while retaining the praise.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3470:Detached not-that qualification blocks an inference
explanation: The detached 'Not that...' unit rejects the suggested implication without withdrawing the preceding description.

rationales.It retracts the praise by treating ingen: The reviewer continues to call the argument ingenious; the qualification limits what follows from that judgment.
rationales.It offers ingenuity as a necessary condi: No necessary-condition claim is made, and ingenuity has already been affirmed.
rationales.It blocks an inference to soundness whil: The detached 'Not that...' unit rejects the suggested implication without withdrawing the preceding description.
rationales.It establishes that the argument is unso: Denying that ingenuity makes an argument sound neither establishes unsoundness nor makes ingenuity its cause.

sentence: Which expansion preserves the final unit's contrast and attachment?
setupText: The editorial reads: 'The promise was simple: access for everyone. The qualifications, less so.'
taskText: Which expansion preserves the final unit's contrast and attachment?
text: The editorial reads: 'The promise was simple: access for everyone. The qualifications, less so.' Which expansion preserves the final unit's contrast and attachment?
options: The qualifications were less simple than the promise.
The qualifications made access less simple for everyone.
The qualifications were less accessible than the promised service.
The qualifications made the promise less applicable to everyone.
answer: The qualifications were less simple than the promise.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3471:Recovering comparative ellipsis across a full stop
explanation: 'Less so' recovers 'less simple'; the omitted linking verb belongs to 'The qualifications'.

rationales.The qualifications made access less simp: This changes a description of the qualifications' complexity into their effect on access.
rationales.The qualifications were less simple than: 'Less so' recovers 'less simple'; the omitted linking verb belongs to 'The qualifications'.
rationales.The qualifications were less accessible: The recovered adjective is 'simple', not 'accessible', which does not occur in the preceding predicate.
rationales.The qualifications made the promise less: This introduces a restriction on applicability rather than the stated contrast in simplicity.

sentence: Which analysis explains why the final that-clause is not an accidental fragment?
setupText: The text reads: 'She had anticipated one response, and one only: that the invitation would be declined.'
taskText: Which analysis explains why the final that-clause is not an accidental fragment?
text: The text reads: 'She had anticipated one response, and one only: that the invitation would be declined.' Which analysis explains why the final that-clause is not an accidental fragment?
options: The clause specifies the anticipated response after a complete introduction.
The colon converts the that-clause into an independent assertion by the narrator.
The colon makes the decline a reason for anticipating a response.
The clause reports a confirmed outcome rather than something anticipated.
answer: The clause specifies the anticipated response after a complete introduction.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3472:Dependent content after a specifying colon retains anticipated status
explanation: A colon can introduce specifying content that is not an independent clause; here it fills out 'one response'.

rationales.The colon converts the that-clause into: The that-clause remains dependent content; a colon does not make it an independently asserted fact.
rationales.The colon makes the decline a reason for: The clause identifies the response itself, not a cause of anticipation.
rationales.The clause specifies the anticipated res: A colon can introduce specifying content that is not an independent clause; here it fills out 'one response'.
rationales.The clause reports a confirmed outcome r: The content stays within what she anticipated; the passage does not say the invitation was actually declined.

sentence: Which assessment identifies what a satisfactory repair must do?
setupText: Draft: 'Having compared the two estimates, the cheaper option seemed preferable.' The client, not an option, made the comparison. The editor suggests merely replacing the comma with a full stop.
taskText: Which assessment identifies what a satisfactory repair must do?
text: Draft: 'Having compared the two estimates, the cheaper option seemed preferable.' The client, not an option, made the comparison. The editor suggests merely replacing the comma with a full stop. Which assessment identifies what a satisfactory repair must do?
options: Make the opening phrase a separate sentence, relying on the following sentence to supply its omitted subject and predicate.
Treat the opener as a conventional writer comment, comparable to 'generally speaking', rather than identifying a comparer.
Replace the comma with a semicolon so the two parts can be interpreted as independent descriptions of the same option.
Reconstruct a complete comparison clause naming the client.
answer: Reconstruct a complete comparison clause naming the client.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3473:Boundary-only editing cannot repair a detached nonfinite agent
explanation: For example, 'The client compared the estimates. The cheaper option seemed preferable' supplies the intended agent and a complete first sentence.

rationales.Make the opening phrase a separate sente: The opening participial phrase would remain a fragment; the full stop does not supply its missing main clause.
rationales.Treat the opener as a conventional write: This phrase describes a specific comparison by a particular person, not a conventional impersonal comment on the writing.
rationales.Replace the comma with a semicolon so th: A semicolon cannot turn 'Having compared...' into an independent clause or identify its intended agent.
rationales.Reconstruct a complete comparison clause: For example, 'The client compared the estimates. The cheaper option seemed preferable' supplies the intended agent and a complete first sentence.

sentence: Why is this comma not simply a comma splice between two independent clauses?
setupText: A report says: 'The windows remained sealed, the ventilation system having failed overnight.'
taskText: Why is this comma not simply a comma splice between two independent clauses?
text: A report says: 'The windows remained sealed, the ventilation system having failed overnight.' Why is this comma not simply a comma splice between two independent clauses?
options: The second unit is an independent past-perfect assertion whose finite auxiliary is recoverable from the preceding clause.
The second unit is a reduced relative that identifies the sealed windows through their ventilation system.
The second unit is a supplementary nonfinite absolute with its own subject.
The second unit supplies the main predicate, while 'The windows remained sealed' functions as its introductory background.
answer: The second unit is a supplementary nonfinite absolute with its own subject.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3474:Comma with an absolute clause versus a true comma splice
explanation: 'The ventilation system' belongs to nonfinite 'having failed'; the comma attaches this background supplement to the main assertion.

rationales.The second unit is a supplementary nonfi: 'The ventilation system' belongs to nonfinite 'having failed'; the comma attaches this background supplement to the main assertion.
rationales.The second unit is an independent past-p: No finite 'had' is omitted or shared here; 'having failed' is a nonfinite construction.
rationales.The second unit is a reduced relative th: The absolute clause has its own subject and does not identify a subset of windows as a relative modifier would.
rationales.The second unit supplies the main predic: 'Remained' is the main finite verb; the nonfinite clause provides background rather than the main predicate.

sentence: What role do the first two units play in the passage?
setupText: A feature writer describes a new terminal: 'More gates. Shorter queues. That was the promise; the opening day told a different story.'
taskText: What role do the first two units play in the passage?
text: A feature writer describes a new terminal: 'More gates. Shorter queues. That was the promise; the opening day told a different story.' What role do the first two units play in the passage?
options: They establish improvements achieved before opening day, which the later sentence says were subsequently lost.
They state the writer's expectations independently of the promise mentioned in the following sentence.
They propose the writer's preferred remedies after the opening-day experience has exposed the terminal's problems.
They compress promised benefits, not verified outcomes.
answer: They compress promised benefits, not verified outcomes.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3475:Later sentence reclassifies preceding fragments as promised content
explanation: The later sentence packages the fragments as a promise and contrasts it with the opening-day experience.

rationales.They establish improvements achieved bef: The backward reference 'That was the promise' frames them as promised results, not achieved improvements.
rationales.They compress promised benefits, not ver: The later sentence packages the fragments as a promise and contrasts it with the opening-day experience.
rationales.They state the writer's expectations ind: The demonstrative 'That' explicitly connects the preceding fragments to the promise.
rationales.They propose the writer's preferred reme: The passage places them within an earlier promise, not a new proposal for remedies.

sentence: Which response best preserves the original action and speech structure under ordinary dialogue conventions?
setupText: A narrative reads: '"I can explain." Mara folded the letter. "But not here."' An editor proposes changing the first full stop to a comma and treating 'Mara folded the letter' as a dialogue tag.
taskText: Which response best preserves the original action and speech structure under ordinary dialogue conventions?
text: A narrative reads: '"I can explain." Mara folded the letter. "But not here."' An editor proposes changing the first full stop to a comma and treating 'Mara folded the letter' as a dialogue tag. Which response best preserves the original action and speech structure under ordinary dialogue conventions?
options: Accept the comma because the speaker's accompanying action can stand in for an omitted 'said' in an ordinary reporting tag.
Keep the action sentence separate; 'folded' does not report speech.
Extend the quotation across the action sentence so that both speech units remain inside one uninterrupted quotation.
Merge the action into the second speech unit so that 'But not here' becomes its grammatical complement.
answer: Keep the action sentence separate; 'folded' does not report speech.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3476:Action beat versus reporting tag at a quotation boundary
explanation: The narrative action stands between two speech units; it does not grammatically attribute either quotation.

rationales.Accept the comma because the speaker's a: An accompanying action beat is not automatically a speech-reporting clause with 'said' omitted.
rationales.Extend the quotation across the action s: That would present the narrator's action description as words spoken by Mara.
rationales.Keep the action sentence separate; 'fold: The narrative action stands between two speech units; it does not grammatically attribute either quotation.
rationales.Merge the action into the second speech: 'But not here' qualifies Mara's ability to explain, not the action of folding the letter.

sentence: Which assessment most accurately distinguishes what the punctuation encodes?
setupText: Original: 'One thing was clear: the producer would not approve the release.' Proposed revision: 'One thing was clear. The producer would not approve the release.'
taskText: Which assessment most accurately distinguishes what the punctuation encodes?
text: Original: 'One thing was clear: the producer would not approve the release.' Proposed revision: 'One thing was clear. The producer would not approve the release.' Which assessment most accurately distinguishes what the punctuation encodes?
options: The full stop removes the writer's commitment that refusal is the particular point being described as clear.
The colon presents refusal as a cause of the writer's clarity, while the full stop changes that cause into a consequence.
The full stop requires the reader to treat the second sentence as another clear point rather than the promised specification.
The colon explicitly specifies 'one thing'; the full stop leaves that link inferable.
answer: The colon explicitly specifies 'one thing'; the full stop leaves that link inferable.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3477:Explicit colon relation versus recoverable relation across a full stop
explanation: Both can convey the same message, but only the colon overtly marks the specifying relationship.

rationales.The full stop removes the writer's commi: The immediate wording still naturally identifies refusal as that point; the full stop does not necessarily withdraw the commitment.
rationales.The colon presents refusal as a cause of: The colon specifies content rather than establishing a cause-and-effect chain.
rationales.The full stop requires the reader to tre: A full stop allows the same discourse connection to be inferred; it does not require a different point.
rationales.The colon explicitly specifies 'one thin: Both can convey the same message, but only the colon overtly marks the specifying relationship.

sentence: What changes in the status of the second alternative?
setupText: Original: 'The team investigated whether the discrepancy reflected a recording error or whether the samples genuinely differed.' Revision: 'The team investigated whether the discrepancy reflected a recording error. Or did the samples genuinely differ?'
taskText: What changes in the status of the second alternative?
text: Original: 'The team investigated whether the discrepancy reflected a recording error or whether the samples genuinely differed.' Revision: 'The team investigated whether the discrepancy reflected a recording error. Or did the samples genuinely differ?' What changes in the status of the second alternative?
options: It becomes a direct question in the narrator's voice rather than an explicitly embedded object of 'investigated'.
It remains explicitly one of the team's investigated alternatives, with only the sentence length changed.
It becomes the team's confirmed explanation of the discrepancy rather than an unresolved alternative.
It is presented as the team's exact question, as though the new sentence boundary supplied quotation marks.
answer: It becomes a direct question in the narrator's voice rather than an explicitly embedded object of 'investigated'.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3478:Boundary and inversion turn an embedded alternative into a narrator's direct question
explanation: The inverted 'did the samples...?' forms an independent direct question; the original kept both alternatives inside the report of the team's investigation.

rationales.It remains explicitly one of the team's: Readers may infer the same research concern, but the full stop and inversion remove the explicit shared reporting structure.
rationales.It becomes a direct question in the narr: The inverted 'did the samples...?' forms an independent direct question; the original kept both alternatives inside the report of the team's investigation.
rationales.It becomes the team's confirmed explanat: A direct question does not confirm that the samples differed; uncertainty remains.
rationales.It is presented as the team's exact ques: The revision does not mark a quotation or identify the wording as the team's exact words.

sentence: How do the comma and semicolon organize the two endorsements?
setupText: The policy summary reads: 'The committee endorsed the principle, though not its immediate implementation; the finance team endorsed neither.'
taskText: How do the comma and semicolon organize the two endorsements?
text: The policy summary reads: 'The committee endorsed the principle, though not its immediate implementation; the finance team endorsed neither.' How do the comma and semicolon organize the two endorsements?
options: The comma conditions the principle's endorsement on implementation, while the semicolon makes the finance team's objection conditional too.
The semicolon extends the committee's concession to the finance team's position, making the latter part of what the committee endorsed.
The comma contains the concession; the semicolon introduces a position on both alternatives.
The comma separates two objects, and the semicolon narrows 'neither' to the later object, immediate implementation.
answer: The comma contains the concession; the semicolon introduces a position on both alternatives.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3479:Layered boundaries around a reduced concession and independent contrast
explanation: The concession stays within the committee's position; the independent finance-team clause uses 'neither' to recover principle and implementation.

rationales.The comma conditions the principle's end: 'Though not' qualifies what was endorsed; it does not establish a condition for endorsement.
rationales.The semicolon extends the committee's co: The finance team supplies a new independent position, not content endorsed by the committee.
rationales.The comma contains the concession; the s: The concession stays within the committee's position; the independent finance-team clause uses 'neither' to recover principle and implementation.
rationales.The comma separates two objects, and the: 'Neither' refers to both contrasted objects rather than being narrowed to one by the boundary.

sentence: Which conclusion about the colon's evidential force is justified?
setupText: A reviewer writes: 'The production promised intimacy: the audience sat within arm's reach of the actors.'
taskText: Which conclusion about the colon's evidential force is justified?
text: A reviewer writes: 'The production promised intimacy: the audience sat within arm's reach of the actors.' Which conclusion about the colon's evidential force is justified?
options: It offers proximity as explanatory detail, not proof of an intimate experience.
It establishes that the physical seating arrangement achieved the intimate experience promised by the production.
It presents the seating arrangement as a factual correction that displaces the production's promise rather than illustrating it.
It attributes the seating claim to the producers' own explanation while withdrawing the reviewer's responsibility for its accuracy.
answer: It offers proximity as explanatory detail, not proof of an intimate experience.
focusKey: coverage-sentence-boundaries-c2-3480:Explanatory colon does not guarantee an asserted detail proves an evaluation
explanation: The colon relates the concrete detail to the promise; it does not itself prove that proximity produced intimacy.

rationales.It establishes that the physical seating: The physical arrangement can support the promise but does not establish the audience's experience.
rationales.It offers proximity as explanatory detai: The colon relates the concrete detail to the promise; it does not itself prove that proximity produced intimacy.
rationales.It presents the seating arrangement as a: The colon presents a close explanatory or illustrative connection, not a correction of the promise.
rationales.It attributes the seating claim to the p: No attribution shifts the seating claim away from the reviewer; the colon is not a quotation or source marker.
